This is hard to explain, at least from an epistemological point of view. Lets say I needed an excuse to dig deeper into a subject that bugged me for the last five months.
Topological Data Analysis (TDA), as I’ve come to understand it, is the belief that data can hold some internal geometric structure that can be exploited through topologist-single-blade-swiss-army-knife homology.
Don’t blame me for the following rant, blame yourself.
The rough idea So the idea is straightforward:
Take any audio file; convert it into its spectrogram. Take the spectrogram and convert it into a point cloud. Take the point cloud and compute its Vietoris-Rips complex. There are several flows already.
Here is a list of self-directed objections: FAQ
Regardlessly, I wrote it anyway. Sit tight.
First of all, how the heck TDA works? Nice and simple. You have your favorite point cloud, right?
Then all you need to do is to grow (hyper-)spheres around them. This is, of course, tailored to the dimensionality of your dataset and the distance you impose on the surrounding space.
Vietoris-Rips Now — hold on.
\(X \) = Programming a visual representation of the Vietoris-Rips complex
I couldn’t do \(X \) by myself in a reasonable amount of time. So I found out someone somewhere has already done a decent approximation of what I imagined \(X \) would be and the MIT licence allows me to COPYPASTA \(X \) .
CREDITS: Cristobal Montecino. Thanks Bro.
Three Stages From Music to Image Ok. Now, how can we massage the information given from an audio file into something we can parse? We have to decide the dimensionality of our data structure, ie we need to choose the what are the type of indipendent information about the file we want to keep track of.
Here is an interactive notebook that computes the spectrogram of a given audio file, curtsy of binder:
or if you fancy google (you need to login to play around):
the code:
import librosa import librosa.display import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import scipy.signal from scipy.io.wavfile import write import numpy as np # import audio file audio_file_path = 'piano.mp3' y, sr = librosa.load(audio_file_path, sr=None) # Load the file as is with its original sampling rate (`sr=None`) # Assuming y and sr are already defined from loading the audio # Compute the Mel-scaled spectrogram S = librosa.feature.melspectrogram(y=y, sr=sr, n_fft=8192, hop_length=128, n_mels=256) S_dB = librosa.power_to_db(S, ref=np.max) # Plot the Mel spectrogram plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8)) librosa.display.specshow(S_dB, sr=sr, x_axis='time', y_axis='mel') # plt.colorbar(format='%+2.0f dB') plt.title('Mel Spectrogram') plt.xlabel('Time') plt.ylabel('Frequency') # plt.tight_layout() # Save the Mel spectrogram to a file plt.savefig('mel_spectrogram.png') From Image to DATA the point cloud
import librosa import librosa.display import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import scipy.signal from scipy.io.wavfile import write import numpy as np from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d import Axes3D # import audio file audio_file_path = 'piano.mp3' y, sr = librosa.load(audio_file_path, sr=None) # Load the file as is with its original sampling rate (`sr=None`) # Assuming you have your audio loaded in `y` and its sampling rate in `sr` S = librosa.feature.melspectrogram(y=y, sr=sr, n_fft=2048, hop_length=512, n_mels=128) S_dB = librosa.power_to_db(S, ref=np.max) # Generate the time and Mel frequency axes times = librosa.times_like(S, sr=sr, hop_length=512) mel_freqs = librosa.mel_frequencies(n_mels=128, fmin=0, fmax=sr/2) # Prepare x (time), y (frequency), and z (intensity) for 3D plotting x = np.tile(times, len(mel_freqs)) y = np.repeat(mel_freqs, len(times)) z = S_dB.flatten() # Plotting fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7)) ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection='3d') # Scatter plot for the 3D point cloud scat = ax.scatter(x, y, z, c=z, cmap='viridis', s=1) # Adding labels and title ax.set_xlabel('Time (s)') ax.set_ylabel('Frequency (Hz)') ax.set_zlabel('Intensity (dB)') ax.set_title('3D Point Cloud of Mel Spectrogram') # Add a color bar to indicate the intensity values cbar = fig.colorbar(scat, ax=ax) cbar.set_label('Intensity (dB)') plt.savefig('mel_pointcloud.png') interactive plot
import librosa import numpy as np import plotly.graph_objects as go # Load your audio and compute the Mel spectrogram y, sr = librosa.load('piano.mp3') S = librosa.feature.melspectrogram(y=y, sr=sr, n_fft=2048, hop_length=512, n_mels=128) S_dB = librosa.power_to_db(S, ref=np.max) # Generate the time and Mel frequency axes times = librosa.times_like(S, sr=sr, hop_length=512) mel_freqs = librosa.mel_frequencies(n_mels=128, fmin=0, fmax=sr/2) # Prepare the data x = np.tile(times, len(mel_freqs)) y = np.repeat(mel_freqs, len(times)) z = S_dB.flatten() # Define the dB threshold for filtering out negligible values db_threshold = -60 # Create a mask to filter out values below the threshold mask = z > db_threshold # Apply the mask to x, y, and z x_filtered = x[mask] y_filtered = y[mask] z_filtered = z[mask] # Create a Plotly scatter3d object with the filtered data fig = go.Figure(data=[go.Scatter3d( x=x_filtered, y=y_filtered, z=z_filtered, mode='markers', marker=dict( size=2, color=z_filtered, # Use filtered intensity for color mapping colorscale='Viridis', opacity=0.8, colorbar=dict(title='Intensity (dB)', bgcolor='black') ) )]) # Update the layout for a better viewing experience in dark mode fig.update_layout( margin=dict(l=0, r=0, b=0, t=0), paper_bgcolor='black', plot_bgcolor='black', scene=dict( xaxis=dict( title='Time (s)', backgroundcolor="black", color='white', gridcolor='gray' ), yaxis=dict( title='Frequency (Hz)', backgroundcolor="black", color='white', gridcolor='gray' ), zaxis=dict( title='Intensity (dB)', backgroundcolor="black", color='white', gridcolor='gray' ) ) ) # Save the plot as an HTML file html_file_path = 'filtered_mel_spectrogram_3d_dark.html' fig.write_html(html_file_path) This is the output:
From DATA to Topology Ok since my 20yo laptop could melt any instant, let’s try to be reasonable and downsample the previous result. This code just divide the space into little cubes and takes the mean value of all the points within.
from ripser import ripser from persim import plot_diagrams, PersistenceImager import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import librosa import plotly.graph_objects as go # Load your audio and compute the Mel spectrogram y, sr = librosa.load('piano.mp3') S = librosa.feature.melspectrogram(y=y, sr=sr, n_fft=2048, hop_length=512, n_mels=128) S_dB = librosa.power_to_db(S, ref=np.max) # Generate the time and Mel frequency axes times = librosa.times_like(S, sr=sr, hop_length=512) mel_freqs = librosa.mel_frequencies(n_mels=128, fmin=0, fmax=sr/2) # Prepare the data x = np.tile(times, len(mel_freqs)) y = np.repeat(mel_freqs, len(times)) z = S_dB.flatten() # Define the dB threshold for filtering out negligible values db_threshold = -60 # Create a mask to filter out values below the threshold mask = z > db_threshold # Apply the mask to x, y, and z x_filtered = x[mask] y_filtered = y[mask] z_filtered = z[mask] # # Create a Plotly scatter3d object with the filtered data # fig = go.Figure(data=[go.Scatter3d( # x=x_filtered, # y=y_filtered, # z=z_filtered, # mode='markers', # marker=dict( # size=2, # color=z_filtered, # Use filtered intensity for color mapping # colorscale='Viridis', # opacity=0.8, # colorbar=dict(title='Intensity (dB)', bgcolor='black') # ) # )]) # Define the downsample by averaging function def downsample_by_averaging(points, cube_size): min_coords = np.min(points, axis=0) max_coords = np.max(points, axis=0) indices = np.floor((points - min_coords) / cube_size).astype(int) dtype = [('sum', float, 3), ('count', int)] grid = np.zeros(indices.max(axis=0) + 1, dtype=dtype) for point, index in zip(points, indices): grid[tuple(index)]['sum'] += point grid[tuple(index)]['count'] += 1 non_empty_cubes = grid['count'] > 0 averaged_points = grid['sum'][non_empty_cubes] / grid['count'][non_empty_cubes][:, np.newaxis] return averaged_points # Assuming x_filtered, y_filtered, and z_filtered are defined and contain your point cloud data points = np.column_stack((x_filtered, y_filtered, z_filtered)) # Combine filtered points and apply downsampling downsampled_points = downsample_by_averaging(points, cube_size=8) # Adjust cube_size as needed # # Plotting the downsampled points with Plotly # fig = go.Figure(data=[go.Scatter3d( # x=downsampled_points[:, 0], # Time # y=downsampled_points[:, 1], # Frequency # z=downsampled_points[:, 2], # Intensity # mode='markers', # marker=dict( # size=2, # color=downsampled_points[:, 2], # Color by intensity # colorscale='Viridis', # opacity=0.8, # ) # )]) # fig.update_layout( # title="Downsampled 3D Mel Spectrogram", # scene=dict( # xaxis_title='Time', # yaxis_title='Frequency', # zaxis_title='Intensity', # ) # ) # #Update the layout for a better viewing experience in dark mode # fig.update_layout( # margin=dict(l=0, r=0, b=0, t=0), # paper_bgcolor='black', # plot_bgcolor='black', # scene=dict( # xaxis=dict( # title='Time (s)', # backgroundcolor="black", # color='white', # gridcolor='gray' # ), # yaxis=dict( # title='Frequency (Hz)', # backgroundcolor="black", # color='white', # gridcolor='gray' # ), # zaxis=dict( # title='Intensity (dB)', # backgroundcolor="black", # color='white', # gridcolor='gray' # ) # ) # ) # # Save the plot as an HTML file # html_file_path = 'downsampled_3D_mel_spectrogram_plot.html' # fig.write_html(html_file_path) # print(f"Plot saved to {html_file_path}") # Assuming downsampled_points is available and contains the downsampled point cloud # Apply Ripser to compute Vietoris-Rips persistence barcodes diagrams = ripser(downsampled_points)['dgms'] # Plot and save the persistence diagrams plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8)) plot_diagrams(diagrams, show=False) plt.savefig('persistence_diagrams_downsampled.png') # plt.close() # Initialize PersistenceImager pimgr = PersistenceImager(pixel_size=0.05) # # Fit and transform the H1 diagram to a persistence image # # Note: diagrams[1] corresponds to H1. Use diagrams[0] for H0. # imgs = pimgr.fit_transform(diagrams[1]) # # Plot and save the persistence image # plt.figure(figsize=(6, 6)) # pimgr.plot_image(imgs[0], ax=plt.gca()) # plt.savefig('persistence_image_downsampled.png') # # plt.close() # Check if the desired homology dimension diagram is non-empty if diagrams[1].size > 0: # Fit and transform to get the persistence image imgs = pimgr.fit_transform([diagrams[1]]) # diagrams[1] for H1 # Plot and save the first (and in this case, only) persistence image plt.imshow(imgs[0], origin='lower', cmap='hot') # plt.colorbar() plt.savefig('persistence_image_downsampled.png') else: print("No features found in the desired homology dimension.") FAQ Why does the spectrogram of an audio file capture its essence? It doesn’t. In my opinion is just an interesting perspective you can take. Besides, it actually simplify a lot the next step.
Wait, but what are spectrograms? TLDW: Spectrograms are the representation in (aplitude, frequency, time)—space of sound.
They encompass so much information about the sound. The key is that by taking only the notes you are basically throwing away all the information about the timbre, i.e. you are effectively restricting to the first Fourier coefficient and silencing to zero every other one.
But Fourier is nice, we want everything. Hence, the Topological Audio-Data Analysis ( TADA! )
Euclidean distance doesn’t capture any “musical” information \(C_{0}\) is musically, perceivably, “closer” to its harmonics than \(D_{0}\), i.e.
\[[C_0, C_1, G_1, C_2, E_2, G_2]\] are the pitches of the first six harmonics in the equal temperament tuning system.
or pedantically the first five overtones: \[[C_1, G_1, C_2, E_2, G_2]\]
and overtones do not have overtones, i.e. are f sine waves. And why is that is f beautiful and Fourier-pilled
What does the information about this “topology” tells about the audio Honestly, I don’t know. But this can be a way to classify the data coming from an audio file. Thinking not that hard about it, you could imagine that no matter the significance of the topological information retrieved in this way, still on a meta-analysis you could find patterns inside classes of similar audio file.
Similarly >> Chris Dumas video
Given that the output is mathematically meaningful, can you recover the topological space from the persistent barcodes? Have somebody else already done it? Kind of:

You weren’t invited, yet here we are.
This isn’t meant for you to read.
The Brain—is wider than the Sky—
For—put them side by side—
The one the other will contain
With ease—and You—beside—
The Brain is deeper than the sea—
For—hold them—Blue to Blue—
The one the other will absorb—
As Sponges—Buckets—do—
The Brain is just the weight of God—
For—Heft them—Pound for Pound—
And they will differ—if they do—
As Syllable from Sound—
— Emily Dickinson
